content: Obstetric ultrasonography, also known as obstetric sonography, is the use of medical ultrasound technology to visualize the embryo or fetus within the uterus of a pregnant woman. This procedure is a routine component of prenatal care, as it provides critical information about the health of both the mother and the fetus, as well as the progression of the pregnancy. Traditional obstetric ultrasounds are performed by placing a transducer, a probe that emits high-frequency sound waves, on the abdomen of the pregnant woman. Another variant, the transvaginal ultrasound, involves inserting a probe into the woman’s vagina. Transvaginal scans are particularly useful in early pregnancy and in cases where the patient is obese, as they often provide clearer images. Doppler ultrasound is another technique used, which detects the fetal heartbeat and evaluates the pulsations in the fetal heart and blood vessels to identify potential abnormalities. In early pregnancy, the gestational sac can sometimes be visualized as early as 4.5 weeks of gestation, which is approximately 2.5 weeks after ovulation. The yolk sac becomes visible around 5 weeks of gestation. By 5.5 weeks, the embryo can be observed and measured, and the heartbeat may be detectable as early as 6 weeks, though it is typically visible by 7 weeks of gestation. Gestational age is generally calculated based on the date of the woman’s last menstrual period, assuming ovulation occurred on the 14th day of the cycle. However, if the date of the last menstrual period is uncertain or ovulation occurred earlier or later than expected, ultrasound scans can provide an alternative method for estimating gestational age. The most accurate measurement for dating is the crown-rump length of the fetus, which is performed between 7 and 13 weeks of gestation. After 13 weeks, fetal age can be estimated using the biparietal diameter (the diameter of the fetal head) and the length of the femur (the longest bone in the body). Dating is more precise when performed earlier in pregnancy. If a later scan provides a different estimate of gestational age, it is generally assumed that the fetus is not growing at the expected rate rather than revising the original estimate. The abdominal circumference of the fetus, while not useful for dating, can be measured to estimate fetal weight and size, which is important for monitoring growth through serial ultrasounds. The sex of the fetus can typically be determined via ultrasound after 16 weeks of gestation, often during the dating scan around 20 weeks. The accuracy of this determination depends on the quality of the ultrasound machine and the skill of the operator. However, ultrasound sex determination is not infallible and may result in false positives or negatives, necessitating careful interpretation of the results. In some countries, routine pregnancy ultrasounds are conducted to screen for developmental abnormalities before birth. These scans assess the status of the fetus’s limbs and vital organs and may include specific tests for abnormalities. Certain abnormalities detected via ultrasound can be addressed through medical treatment in utero or managed with specialized perinatal care. In some cases, findings may lead to decisions regarding pregnancy termination. One common screening test is the measurement of nuchal translucency thickness, also known as the NT test or Nuchal Scan. While 91% of fetuses with Down syndrome exhibit this abnormality, 5% of fetuses flagged by the test are actually normal. The history of obstetric ultrasound dates back to 1962, when Joseph Holmes, William Wright, and Ralph Meyerdirk developed the first compound contact B-mode scanner after two years of work. In 1963, the Public Health Services and the University of Colorado introduced the first commercial hand-held articulated arm compound contact B-mode scanner, which became the most popular design in the history of ultrasound scanners. Obstetric ultrasound has significantly contributed to the advancement of diagnostic ultrasound technology, with many technological improvements driven by the need for better obstetric equipment. For example, Acuson Corporation’s pioneering work on Coherent Image Formation has influenced the development of diagnostic ultrasound equipment as a whole. Current evidence suggests that diagnostic ultrasound is safe for the unborn child, unlike radiographs, which use ionizing radiation. However, no randomized controlled trials have been conducted to definitively test the safety of ultrasound technology. As a result, ultrasound procedures are generally not performed repeatedly unless medically necessary. A 2006 study on mice exposed to ultrasound revealed neurological changes in the exposed fetuses, with some brain cells failing to migrate to their proper positions and remaining scattered in incorrect areas of the brain.
